conventional_description: Silicosis is a progressive occupational lung disease caused by inhaling tiny particles of crystalline silica dust, typically from mining, construction, or manufacturing. Over years or decades, these particles lodge deep in the lungs, triggering inflammation and irreversible scarring (fibrosis) that stiffens the lung tissue. Common symptoms include chronic dry cough, shortness of breath with exertion, fatigue, and increased susceptibility to respiratory infections. Diagnosis is based on a history of silica exposure, chest X-ray or CT scan showing characteristic nodules or masses, and pulmonary function tests.
conventional_treatments: There is no cure for silicosis, and the lung scarring cannot be reversed. Management focuses on preventing further exposure, symptom relief, and slowing progression. This includes bronchodilators for wheezing, oxygen therapy for low blood oxygen levels, vaccinations to prevent respiratory infections, and prompt antibiotic treatment for infections. In advanced cases, lung transplantation may be considered. Pulmonary rehabilitation programs help maintain exercise capacity and quality of life.
tcm_understanding:
In Chinese medicine, silicosis begins with an invasion of external pathogens - the tiny silica dust particles inhaled over years act as a toxic, sticky substance that the Lungs cannot clear. This dust lodges deep in the Lung tissue, obstructing the normal flow of Qi and body fluids. The Lungs, which govern the descending and dispersing of Qi, become congested, and the trapped fluids congeal into Dampness and then thick Phlegm. This is why the earliest and most common TCM pattern is Damp-Phlegm in the Lungs, marked by copious white, sticky sputum and a heavy sensation in the chest.
When the stagnant Phlegm sits too long or when an external infection strikes, it can transform into Heat, creating the Phlegm-Heat pattern. The sputum turns yellow or green, the chest feels tight and hot, and fever may appear. This is the TCM understanding of an acute flare or superimposed infection in a silicosis patient. The tongue becomes red with a greasy yellow coat, and the pulse turns rapid and slippery. Treating this pattern requires clearing Heat while still transforming Phlegm - a different strategy than the drying approach used for cold Damp-Phlegm.
As the disease wears on, the constant burden of fighting the dust pathogen depletes the body's core energy. The Lungs weaken, and because the Spleen is the source of Qi, it too becomes exhausted, leading to Spleen and Lung Qi Deficiency. The cough becomes weak, fatigue is profound, and the patient catches every cold. In the later fibrotic stages, years of Qi stagnation cause Blood Stagnation - the dark, fixed pain and purplish tongue that reflect scarred, poorly circulated tissue. Eventually, the Kidneys and even the Heart can become involved, as the Kidneys fail to grasp the Lung Qi downward, causing severe breathlessness and palpitations.
This progression explains why silicosis is not one pattern but a sequence of overlapping patterns that can shift over time. A patient may have Damp-Phlegm as a baseline, flare into Phlegm-Heat during an infection, and simultaneously suffer from underlying Qi deficiency. TCM diagnosis carefully reads the sputum, the tongue, and the pulse to determine which pattern is dominant at any given moment, allowing treatment to be precisely targeted.
classical_quote: 「肺痿之病，从何得之？师曰：或从汗出，或从呕吐，或从消渴，小便利数，或从便难，又被快药下利，重亡津液，故得之。」
classical_translation: "How does the disease of lung atrophy arise? The master says: It may follow profuse sweating, repeated vomiting, wasting-thirst with frequent urination, or difficult defecation treated with harsh purgatives - all cause severe loss of fluids, and thus it arises."
classical_source:
Jin Gui Yao Lue (Essentials from the Golden Cabinet)  ,  Chapter 7: On Lung Atrophy, Lung Abscess, Cough, and Upper-Breath Disease 									·

tcm_diagnosis:
A practitioner first asks about the sputum. If it is white, sticky, and copious, with a sensation of fullness in the chest, the picture points toward Damp-Phlegm in the Lungs. This is the most common early pattern in silicosis, where the inhaled dust has congealed into dampness. The tongue coating is thick and greasy, and the pulse feels slippery, like beads rolling under the finger.
When an acute flare or infection occurs, the picture shifts sharply. Sputum turns yellow and sticky, and the person may feel feverish with a tight, oppressive sensation in the chest. This is Phlegm-Heat in the Lungs. The tongue becomes red with a yellow greasy coat, and the pulse turns rapid and slippery. The practitioner looks for this pattern to decide whether to focus on clearing heat rather than just drying dampness.
As the disease wears on, the body’s energy runs low. The cough becomes weak and the sputum thin. Breathlessness and fatigue dominate, and the person catches colds easily. This is Spleen and Lung Qi Deficiency. The tongue looks pale and the pulse is weak and thready. The practitioner checks for this pattern to gauge how much the body’s core strength has been depleted, which changes the treatment from clearing phlegm to building Qi.
Later, the lungs become stiff and scarred, and a fixed, stabbing chest pain emerges. The sputum may be hard to cough out and tinged with blood. This points to Blood Stagnation. The tongue appears purplish with stasis spots, and the pulse is choppy. The practitioner identifies this pattern to add herbs that move blood and soften the hardened tissue, rather than only addressing phlegm.
In advanced silicosis, the whole system weakens. Palpitations, insomnia, severe fatigue, and lower back soreness signal that the heart and kidneys are involved. This is Kidney and Heart Qi Deficiency. The tongue is pale with a thin coat, and the pulse is deep and weak. The practitioner looks for this pattern to support the deepest reserves of the body, as the condition has moved beyond the lungs.

patterns.symptoms: ["Copious white sticky phlegm that is easy to expectorate", "Chest heaviness and tightness", "Poor appetite and bloating after eating", "Heavy, tired feeling in the whole body"]
patterns.worse_with: Cold or damp weather, Greasy, fried, or dairy foods, Sedentary lifestyle, Overeating or heavy meals, Exposure to dust or smoke, Excessive worry
patterns.better_with: Warmth, Gentle exercise, Dry, airy rooms, Warm, light meals, Rest
patterns.why_this_happens: Inhaled silica dust acts as a heavy, sticky external pathogen that settles in the Lungs and obstructs the flow of Qi. The Lungs lose their ability to descend and disperse fluids, so body fluids congeal into Dampness and then thick Phlegm. The Spleen, overwhelmed by the burden of processing this sticky Phlegm, also weakens, creating a cycle that fills the chest with copious white sputum and a heavy, congested sensation.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Pale, swollen body with teeth marks and a thick white greasy coating. Pulse: Slippery (hua, 滑), like beads rolling beneath the fingers.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Damp-Phlegm is a cold, heavy, and sticky pathogen that obstructs the Lungs. Cold and damp environments add external Dampness, worsening the condition. Greasy and dairy foods create internal Dampness and burden the Spleen, leading to more Phlegm. Sedentary habits allow Qi to stagnate, while gentle movement helps Qi flow and transforms Dampness. Warmth and dry air help disperse the cold, sticky Phlegm, while light, warm foods support Spleen function and reduce phlegm production.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid cold, raw, and greasy foods, as well as dairy, which all promote Dampness and Phlegm. Eat warm, cooked meals like congee, soups, and lightly steamed vegetables. Ginger tea can help warm the Lungs and transform Phlegm. Gentle daily movement such as walking or tai chi helps Qi flow and prevents stagnation, but avoid overexertion.

patterns.why_this_happens: Inhaled silica dust settles deep in the Lungs, damaging their ability to spread and descend Qi and fluids. This trapped fluid thickens into Phlegm. When the Phlegm stagnates for too long, it generates Heat, or an external infection combines with the internal Phlegm to create Phlegm-Heat. The Heat and sticky Phlegm block the airways, producing the hallmark yellow phlegm, chest oppression, and fever seen during acute flare-ups of silicosis.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, possibly swollen at the front, with a yellow greasy coating and red prickles on the front third. Pulse: slippery (hua) and rapid (shu), strongest at the right cun position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Phlegm-Heat thrives on anything that adds Heat or thickens Phlegm. Spicy and greasy foods, hot environments, and smoking all fuel Heat and Phlegm formation. Emotional stress, especially anger, stirs up Fire, which can combine with Phlegm. Cooling foods and rest help clear Heat, while pears and radish specifically thin and expel Phlegm. Avoiding dust and smoke removes the very irritants that triggered the condition, giving the Lungs a chance to recover.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid greasy, spicy, and heating foods that generate Phlegm and Heat. Eat cooling, phlegm-resolving foods like pear, radish, and water chestnut. Stay well hydrated. Minimize exposure to dust, smoke, and hot, humid environments. Gentle breathing exercises can help keep the airways open.

patterns.why_this_happens: In silicosis, inhaled silica dust first damages the Lungs, weakening their ability to descend Qi and causing a chronic, weak cough. Over time, the Lungs draw heavily on the Spleen - the source of Qi - which becomes depleted, leading to poor appetite, bloating, and loose stools. The combined deficiency results in profound fatigue, a soft voice, and breathlessness that worsens with even mild exertion, reflecting the progressive decline in both respiratory and digestive energy.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, and tender with teeth marks and a thin white coating. Pulse: overall weak and forceless, especially in the right cun (Lung) and right guan (Spleen) positions, which feel empty.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: This pattern is rooted in a deep deficit of Qi. Overwork and physical exhaustion drain the already scarce Qi, while raw, cold foods extinguish the Spleen's digestive fire, leading to more phlegm and fatigue. Worry directly knots the Spleen Qi. Conversely, rest allows the body to conserve and rebuild Qi; warm, cooked foods are easily transformed into energy; and gentle exercise like qigong moves Qi without depleting it, while avoiding drafts protects the Lung's defensive Qi.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked, easily digestible meals like soups and congees. Avoid raw, cold, and greasy foods that tax the Spleen. Gentle daily movement such as walking or qigong helps circulate Qi without exhausting it. Protect yourself from wind and cold to prevent respiratory infections.

patterns.worse_with: Cold or damp weather, Sedentary lifestyle, Emotional stress, Cold or raw foods

patterns.why_this_happens: In silicosis, inhaled silica dust acts as a stubborn pathogen that lodges in the Lung collaterals, obstructing the smooth flow of Qi and Blood over many years. As the disease progresses into the fibrotic stage, the chronic stagnation congeals into Blood Stasis. This produces the hallmark fixed, stabbing chest pain and the purplish discoloration of the tongue, lips, and nail beds, reflecting blood that is no longer moving freely through the chest.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: dark purple body, possible stasis spots, distended dark sublingual veins, thin white coat. Pulse: choppy (Se) or wiry (Xian).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Blood Stasis means the blood is thick and sluggish, like traffic in a jam. Cold and inactivity make it congeal further, while warmth and gentle movement help it flow. Emotional stress tightens the Liver Qi, which governs the smooth circulation of Blood, worsening the stagnation. So warming, moving, and relaxing habits are key to breaking up the stasis and easing the chest pain.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warming, blood-moving foods like turmeric, ginger, garlic, black fungus, and a small amount of saffron. Avoid cold and raw foods that congeal the blood. Gentle daily movement such as walking or Qi Gong is essential to keep circulation flowing. Strictly avoid further dust exposure and smoking, which damage the Lung collaterals.

patterns.why_this_happens: In advanced silicosis, years of inhaled silica dust have deeply damaged the Lungs, exhausting Lung Qi. The Lungs govern Qi, and the Kidneys are supposed to grasp that Qi and anchor it downward. When Lung Qi collapses, the Kidneys lose their ability to receive Qi, leading to severe shortness of breath on the slightest activity and a deep, aching weakness in the lower back and knees. Because the Heart and Kidneys share a fundamental connection through the Shao Yin channels, depleted Kidney Qi fails to support Heart Qi, causing palpitations, restless sleep, poor memory, and a profound fatigue that rest does not fix.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, and tender with tooth marks; thin white coating. Pulse: fine and weak, especially at the left cun (Heart) and both chi (Kidney) positions.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Physical activity and prolonged standing drain the already depleted Kidney and Heart Qi, triggering breathlessness and palpitations. Rest and lying down conserve Qi and allow the Kidneys to anchor it. Cold constricts and consumes Yang Qi, while warmth helps Qi move and protects the Kidneys. Overeating burdens the Spleen, which is the source of postnatal Qi, so small warm meals support rather than exhaust the body's energy supply. Gentle breathing exercises help the Lungs descend Qi to the Kidneys without overexertion.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, easy-to-digest foods like congee, stews, and root vegetables to protect the Spleen and build Qi. Avoid raw, cold, and greasy foods that drain digestive fire. Gentle breathing exercises and very light walking can help Qi flow without depleting it; stop well before you feel tired. Prioritize deep rest and keep the lower back warm.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture help with silicosis breathing difficulties?
faqs.answer: Yes, acupuncture can help open the chest and improve breathing by relaxing the muscles around the ribcage and calming the nervous system. Points on the back (such as Feishu BL-13) and chest (like Danzhong CV-17) are used to strengthen Lung function and transform phlegm. Many patients notice easier, deeper breathing after a series of treatments, though the effect is supportive rather than curative.

faqs.question: Are Chinese herbs safe with my oxygen therapy?
faqs.answer: In general, yes. Herbal formulas are taken orally and do not interfere with supplemental oxygen. However, you should always inform both your TCM practitioner and your pulmonologist about all therapies you are using. Some herbs may have mild effects on blood pressure or circulation, so coordination of care is important, especially if you have advanced disease.

faqs.question: How long does it take to see results from TCM treatment?
faqs.answer: Most patients notice some improvement in phlegm and cough within the first 4-8 weeks. Energy levels and resistance to infection typically improve more gradually over 3-6 months. TCM does not reverse existing scarring, so the goal is to slow progression, manage symptoms, and enhance quality of life. Consistency with herbs and acupuncture appointments is key to seeing steady progress.

faqs.question: Will TCM reverse the scarring in my lungs?
faqs.answer: TCM cannot reverse established fibrotic scarring. However, by transforming phlegm, moving blood stasis, and strengthening Lung and Kidney Qi, treatment may help slow further fibrotic changes and improve the function of remaining healthy lung tissue. Patients often report less breathlessness and fewer infections, which can make a meaningful difference in daily life.

faqs.question: Do I need to change my diet while taking Chinese herbs?
faqs.answer: Diet plays a supporting role. In general, you'll want to avoid cold, raw, and greasy foods that burden the Spleen and generate more phlegm. Dairy, sugar, and excessive wheat can increase phlegm production for many people. Warm, cooked foods like congee, soups, and steamed vegetables are encouraged, along with pears and white fungus to moisten the Lungs without creating Dampness. Your practitioner will give you specific guidance based on your pattern.

faqs.question: Can I use TCM alongside my bronchodilators and other medications?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM is typically used as a complementary therapy. Herbs and acupuncture can work alongside inhalers and other medications without known major interactions. However, some herbs that move blood may have mild blood-thinning properties, so if you take anticoagulants, inform both your TCM practitioner and your doctor. Never stop or adjust your prescribed medications without consulting your physician.

research.title: Research progress of Chinese medicine pulmonary rehabilitation technique in treatment of pneumoconiosis
research.description: A comprehensive review of TCM pulmonary rehabilitation for pneumoconiosis, summarizing evidence from herbal medicine, acupuncture, acupoint application, and traditional exercise therapies. The review found that TCM interventions improve clinical symptoms, exercise tolerance, and quality of life, and may slow disease progression when combined with conventional treatment.
research.periodical: Liang XB, Li SY, Chen D. Research progress of Chinese medicine pulmonary rehabilitation technique in treatment of pneumoconiosis. Occup Health & Emerg Rescue. 2024;42(4):533-538.

research.title: Clinical observation on modified Bufei Decoction for pneumoconiosis with lung qi deficiency
research.description: An RCT of 74 pneumoconiosis patients with lung qi deficiency. The group receiving modified Bufei Decoction plus standard care showed significantly greater improvement in TCM symptom scores, COPD assessment test scores, and lung function parameters compared to standard care alone, suggesting the formula can reduce inflammation and oxidative stress.
research.periodical: Gong XW, et al. Clinical observation on modified Bufei Decoction for pneumoconiosis with lung qi deficiency. Chin J Ind Med. 2019;36(3):345-348.

research.title: Clinical efficacy of Guben Yifei Decoction for pneumoconiosis with lung-kidney qi deficiency
research.description: A clinical trial evaluating Guben Yifei Decoction in patients with pneumoconiosis and lung-kidney qi deficiency. The herbal group demonstrated marked relief of cough, sputum, and shortness of breath, and an increase in 6-minute walk distance, indicating improved functional capacity and quality of life.
research.periodical: Li YT. Clinical efficacy of Guben Yifei Decoction for pneumoconiosis with lung-kidney qi deficiency. J Tradit Chin Med. 2020;38(2):112-115.
